detail:
Exercise is uniformly recommended across sources as a first-line reconditioning approach for POTS. In a small study by Fu et al. (reported in the journal Hypertension), 19 patients completed 3 months of training that began with 30–45-minute recumbent sessions 2–4 times per week — using a recumbent bike, rowing, or swimming — and progressed to 5–6 hours per week, with upright exercise added in months 2–3. Of those 19 completers, 10 (53%) no longer met the diagnostic criteria for POTS after the program. This is reported for the small study's completers and is not presented as a cure.

A 2024 review in the Journal of Clinical Medicine offers a caution: nearly 60% of enrolled patients could not complete the high-intensity Dallas protocol, indicating that programs need to be individualized to the patient's capacity. Dr. Benjamin Levine is quoted saying patients "will need to incorporate the training program into their everyday lives indefinitely" to maintain the benefits.

Talk to your doctor before starting any exercise program for POTS.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material.
sourceVideoTitle: Exercise training shows promise for POTS patients
summary: Sources uniformly describe exercise as a first-line reconditioning approach for POTS, usually starting in recumbent positions; evidence comes from small studies, and programs must be individualized.

A 2024 Journal of Clinical Medicine review notes nearly 60% of enrolled patients could not complete the high-intensity Dallas protocol, so programs need to be individualized.

Dr. Levine is quoted saying patients "will need to incorporate the training program into their everyday lives indefinitely" to maintain benefits. Talk to your doctor before starting an exercise program.
